briefing.text: The mutation table seems to hold only tumour-tissue barcodes (CD##), with no plasma sample, sample-type field or plasma VAF. Check this first. If it holds, the share of tumours with a tissue mutation at each stage is not cfDNA detection. Nearly every tumour carries tissue mutations, so a flat rate across stages says nothing about cfDNA and must not be read as contradicting the claim.
briefing.reason: This stops the teams from treating tissue mutation presence as if it were cfDNA detection, which would give a misleading flat result.

briefing.text: The hypothesis is an 'and/or' claim: advanced stage, high tumour volume and/or aggressive histology. The clinical table appears to have histology, grade, LVSI, surgical stage and TMB, and no tumour size or volume column. A missing volume variable alone does not make the claim untestable. Test the parts you can (stage, histology, LVSI). LVSI and advanced stage are reasonable stand-ins for tumour burden.
briefing.reason: Without this, the teams may answer Not verifiable, or require all three components, just because volume is missing.

briefing.text: Do not use TMB or mutation count as a stand-in for aggressiveness or for how detectable cfDNA is. In endometrial cancer, hypermutated (POLE/MSI) tumours are often low-grade endometrioid with a good prognosis. Use stage, histology and LVSI instead.
briefing.reason: TMB is the only numeric variable and it is tempting to use, but it points the wrong way.

briefing.text: Define aggressive histology by tumour type, not by the grade column. Grade is blank for types that are high grade by nature: serous, carcinosarcoma, high-grade carcinoma, de-differentiated. Crosstab histologic subtype by grade. High-risk = serous, carcinosarcoma, HG carcinoma, de-differentiated, mixed, high-grade adenosarcoma and grade 3 endometrioid. Low-risk = grade 1-2 endometrioid.
briefing.reason: If blank grade is treated as missing or low, the most aggressive cases are misclassified or dropped.

briefing.text: The stage column is misspelled SURGIVAL_STAGE and holds non-standard values such as 'IA + ITC', 'IB + ITC', 'IVB*', 'IIIC1' and 'IIIC2'. LVSI has an 'NP' value. List the unique values first. Remove '+ ITC' (under FIGO 2009, isolated tumour cells do not raise the stage, so these are stage I) and remove '*'. Treat LVSI 'NP' as missing. The library proposed two cut-points: I vs II-IV and I-II vs III-IV. Fix one before you look at any result (III-IV is the usual meaning of 'advanced' in endometrial cancer) and report the other only as a sensitivity check.
briefing.reason: Matching the raw strings exactly would create spurious categories. Choosing the cut-point after seeing the data would bias the test.

briefing.text: If cfDNA cannot be tested directly, the label rests on established biology, and the reasoning must say so. The web was unavailable, so this comes from the library's prior knowledge only, with medium confidence. Tumour-informed cfDNA studies (Bettegowda 2014; Abbosh 2017 TRACERx; endometrial cfDNA cohorts) report that preoperative ctDNA detection rises with stage, tumour size/volume, high grade, aggressive non-endometrioid histology and LVSI. Detection in early, low-grade disease is described as uncommon.
briefing.reason: The task convention says to decide from established biology when the tables cannot test a claim directly. This is the main prior on which the decision rests.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed the hypothesis is the study's original finding rather than its reversal; neither tested this against the cohort's make-up. Most cases are stage IA, low-grade endometrioid, LVSI-negative tumours, so a study built this way could just as well report detection in early, low-risk disease, or detection limited to high-risk cases.
Both treated 'ctDNA detection scales with stage, burden and histology' as settled biology and used it to decide the label. That is a general prior, not something checked against this cohort.
Both took every row in the mutation table to be tumour tissue, because barcodes equal patient IDs. Neither checked whether any rows are matched cfDNA calls.
unused_evidence: The t_ref_count, t_alt_count, n_ref_count and n_alt_count columns are present but appear empty. Neither team noted this or checked whether any variant has allele-fraction information that could separate tissue calls from plasma calls.
The '+ ITC' and '*' (as in 'IVB*') annotations in the stage column were not explained. Team B grouped ITC cases as early stage without testing whether that changes the high-risk grouping.

TMB was set aside on a library fact about its direction. Its distribution by histology (high TMB in endometrioid cases, likely MSI/POLE) was not used to think about which tumours the study could track.
The 'High grade' adenosarcoma and 'Mixed' grade 3 cases need an explicit risk assignment. The grade column is blank for non-endometrioid types.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A: the label rests on the benchmark convention and biology, not on the data. This was reported, not resolved.
Team B: it named the reversal risk (pitfall 'Reversed-wording check against cohort composition', found_in_data false) but did not resolve it.
second_readings: The hypothesis can be read as a restriction: detection happens only, or mainly, in advanced, high-volume or aggressive cases. It can also be read as 'detection happens in these patients', which says nothing about early-stage cases. The two readings call for different evidence. A cohort dominated by early-stage cases makes the restrictive reading's reversal ('also detected in early-stage, low-grade disease') a real candidate.
'And/or' joins three criteria, one of which (tumour volume) has no variable in the tables. It is unclear whether the claim fails if any one part fails.
challenge.verdict: I trust the agreed answer only moderately. Neither team has deposited cfDNA data, so both labels rest on the assumption, shared and untested, that the hypothesis is the original finding and not its reversal. A cohort made up mostly of early-stage, low-grade cases makes that assumption worth checking.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Tabulate how many cases are low-risk (stage I, endometrioid grade 1-2, no LVSI) versus high-risk. Given that make-up, does the study's design look built to show detection limited to high-risk cases, or detection across early-stage disease? Does that change whether you read the hypothesis as the original finding or its reversal?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Check whether t_ref_count, t_alt_count, n_ref_count, n_alt_count or any other column in the mutation table holds values for any row. If all are empty, does that leave anything in the data that bears on the label beyond study context?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your label leans on 'established ctDNA biology'. Can you name which part of that biology is specific to preoperative endometrial cancer, as opposed to ctDNA in advanced solid tumours generally? If it is not specific, does your confidence change?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You listed 'Reversed-wording check against cohort composition' as not found. Run it now: count stage IA low-grade endometrioid cases against stage III-IV or non-endometrioid cases. Does that make the hypothesis look like the paper's finding or its reversal, and does it change your label?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Re-run your stage by histology crosstab with the '+ ITC' cases and the 'IVB*' case coded each possible way. Does the high-risk group's membership, or your reading of it, change?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: The hypothesis says 'and/or', and tumour volume has no variable. Does your label hold if the claim is read as requiring all three criteria, and also if detection outside those groups (early-stage, low-grade) would count against it?

questions.why: Both teams decided the label from general ctDNA biology. Evidence specific to endometrial cancer would show whether the restrictive reading or its reversal is better supported.

questions.why: How the ITC-annotated stage cases are grouped determines who counts as advanced stage.

findings.question: In published studies of preoperative circulating tumour DNA in endometrial cancer, how often is ctDNA detected in early-stage, low-grade endometrioid tumours compared with advanced-stage or non-endometrioid tumours?
findings.answer: Not settled by the web: every search/contents call returned HTTP 403, so no page was read. From prior knowledge only: endometrial cfDNA studies report preoperative ctDNA detection mostly in advanced-stage, LVSI-positive, high-volume or non-endometrioid/high-grade tumours, and less often (though not never) in early-stage low-grade endometrioid tumours. This supports the hypothesis as stated, not its reversal.

findings.question: In FIGO 2009 endometrial cancer staging, how are isolated tumour cells in lymph nodes recorded, and are such cases usually counted as node-negative early-stage disease in risk grouping?
findings.answer: Not settled by the web (HTTP 403 on every call). From prior knowledge only: FIGO 2009 has no explicit ITC rule. Under AJCC/TNM convention, ITCs (<=0.2 mm) are recorded as pN0(i+) and do not upstage, and FIGO 2023 says this explicitly. So stage I cases annotated with ITC count as node-negative early-stage disease. Micrometastases (>0.2-2 mm) count as stage IIIC.
